theme: 3 terms on control flow and leaving code early

terms.definition: A Bool expression that Swift checks to decide which path the code takes.
terms.example: The if only runs when the condition is true, so log the value to see why it never fires.

terms.definition: A Swift statement that checks a condition and must leave the current scope if the check fails.
terms.example: Use a guard at the top of the method so we bail out when the user is not signed in.

terms.definition: A style of returning from a function as soon as a requirement fails, so the main code stays unindented.
terms.example: I rewrote the nested ifs as an early exit, and now the happy path reads straight down.

video.description:
Learn to talk about control flow in Swift: Condition, guard and Early Exit, with real code, a quiz at the end and each example read twice (normal, then slow).

Today's terms
Condition - A Bool expression that Swift checks to decide which path the code takes.
guard - A Swift statement that checks a condition and must leave the current scope if the check fails.
Early Exit - A style of returning from a function as soon as a requirement fails, so the main code stays unindented.

Quiz at the end - write your answers in the comments, then watch again to check.

landscape.description:
Explain conditions, guard and early exit in Swift by listening to a real code review chat between two iOS devs.

Condition - A Bool expression that Swift checks to decide which path the code takes.
한국어: 코드가 어느 길로 갈지 정하기 위해 Swift가 확인하는 Bool 식

guard - A Swift statement that checks a condition and must leave the current scope if the check fails.
한국어: 조건을 확인하고, 실패하면 현재 범위를 반드시 벗어나게 하는 구문

한국어: 조건이 맞지 않으면 바로 반환해서 메인 코드를 들여쓰기 없이 두는 스타일

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Jake, this login method has five nested ifs. I got lost on line ten.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: I know. Every if checks one thing, so the code moves to the right.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Let's read the first condition. What does it check?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: It checks if the user is signed in. If the condition is true, the code continues.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: And when the condition is false, the else is at the very bottom, thirty lines later.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Yes, that is hard to read. What do you suggest?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Use guard. A guard checks a condition at the top, and if it fails, you leave.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So I write guard isSignedIn else, and then return.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes. The else block of a guard must leave the scope. Swift forces you to do that.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What if I forget the return? Does it build?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: No. The compiler shows an error. That is a good safety net.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Nice. So this is what people call an early exit.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Right. An early exit means you stop as soon as a requirement fails.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Then the early exit keeps the main code on the left side, with no indent.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Exactly. The happy path reads straight down.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: I disagree on one thing. For a simple true or false choice, I still like a plain if.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Fair. Use if for choices, and use guard for requirements.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Deal. A clear condition, a guard, and an early exit.
The if never runs, so log the condition and check it.
